Pre-norm vs post-norm and why depth needs pre-norm
RMSNorm and how it differs from LayerNorm

intro.why: Today's LLMs are still Transformers, but nearly every component has been quietly upgraded. These four changes (normalisation, positional encoding, activation, and sparse experts) are in almost every modern model card, and they explain differences in training stability, context length and cost.
prereq: Transformer block: attention + feed-forward + residuals (recapped in M8)

sections.title: Pre-norm vs post-norm
sections.plain: Normalise the input of each sub-layer rather than the output, so very deep stacks train stably.
sections.body:
The Transformer block has been improved in many small ways, each making training more stable, cheaper or more capable. Start with where normalisation sits. The original Transformer used post-norm:

$$h \leftarrow \text{Norm}(h + F(h))\qquad\text{vs pre-norm}\qquad h \leftarrow h + F(\text{Norm}(h))$$

In pre-norm the residual stream h passes from the first layer to the last untouched by any normalisation: a clean identity path that carries gradients straight back to early layers. Post-norm forces every gradient through every norm, so deep post-norm models need careful learning-rate warm-up and can diverge. Modern LLMs use pre-norm (plus one final norm before the output layer). Trade-off: in pre-norm the stream's scale grows slowly with depth, which the final norm handles.

sections.title: RMSNorm
sections.plain: Scale by the root-mean-square and skip subtracting the mean: cheaper, equally good.
sections.body:
LayerNorm: $\hat x_i = \gamma_i (x_i - \mu)/\sigma + \beta_i$. RMSNorm drops the mean subtraction and the bias:

$$\hat x_i = \gamma_i\,\frac{x_i}{\sqrt{\tfrac1d\sum_j x_j^2 + \epsilon}}$$

Worked: x = [2, −1, 3, 0]. LayerNorm (mean 1, std 1.58) → [0.63, −1.26, 1.26, −0.63]. RMSNorm (RMS 1.87) → [1.07, −0.53, 1.60, 0]. RMSNorm saves one reduction and subtraction per call, a few percent of runtime at the scale of billions of calls, with no measurable loss in quality: re-centring turns out not to matter, re-scaling does.

sections.title: Rotary position embedding (RoPE)
sections.plain: Rotate queries and keys by an angle set by position, so attention scores depend on relative distance.
sections.body:
Attention has no built-in sense of order. Instead of adding a position vector to the input, RoPE rotates each 2-D pair of query and key dimensions by an angle proportional to position:

$$\begin{pmatrix}q'_{2i}\\ q'_{2i+1}\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos m\theta_i & -\sin m\theta_i\\ \sin m\theta_i & \cos m\theta_i\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}q_{2i}\\ q_{2i+1}\end{pmatrix},\qquad \theta_i = 10000^{-2i/d}$$

Because rotating q by mθ and k by nθ leaves an angle of (m − n)θ between them, $q'_m\cdot k'_n$ depends only on the relative distance m − n. In code example ex1, the same q and k give score −2.6427 at positions (3, 1), (10, 8) and (105, 103). Rotation preserves vector length, so content strength isn't distorted.

Picture each word on a clock face at an angle set by its position: words the same distance apart always have the same angle between them. Relative encoding generalises better to long sequences, and RoPE's frequencies can be rescaled to extend context (M16).

sections.title: GELU and gated linear units
sections.plain: Smooth activations instead of ReLU's sharp corner, and gates that let the network choose what passes.
sections.body:
The feed-forward network needs a non-linearity. GELU, $z\,\Phi(z)$, is a smooth version of ReLU: near zero it lets small negative values through (GELU(−0.5) ≈ −0.154) and has no kink, giving better-behaved gradients. GPT-2 and BERT use it. SiLU/Swish, $z\,\sigma(z)$, is similar (SiLU(−0.5) ≈ −0.189).

Gated Linear Units multiply two linear projections, one passed through a gate function:

$$\text{GLU}(x) = \sigma(W_g x) \odot (W_u x)$$

The gate decides, per hidden unit and per input, how much of the content projection passes: a learned, data-dependent filter rather than a fixed curve.

sections.title: SwiGLU feed-forward layers
sections.plain: Use a SiLU gate inside a GLU; with width adjusted, it beats a plain GELU MLP at the same size.
sections.body:
$$\text{FFN}_{\text{SwiGLU}}(x) = W_{\text{down}}\big[\,\text{SiLU}(W_{\text{gate}}x)\odot W_{\text{up}}x\,\big]$$

SwiGLU has three weight matrices instead of two, so the hidden width is reduced to about 2/3 (from 4d to ≈ 8d/3) to keep parameters equal: with d = 4096, a plain MLP has 2·d·4d ≈ 134.2M parameters and SwiGLU 3·d·(8d/3) ≈ 134.2M. For the same size it consistently reaches lower loss, which is why it is now standard (PaLM, Llama and most recent open models).

Why gating helps is partly empirical; the multiplicative interaction lets features switch each other on and off, making the layer more expressive per parameter.

sections.title: Mixture of Experts routing
sections.plain: Replace one feed-forward network with many experts and run only the top few for each token.
sections.body:
Mixture of Experts makes models bigger without making each token slower. Each MoE layer has E expert FFNs and a small gating (router) network. For token x: compute gate scores $g = \text{softmax}(W_r x)$, keep the top-k experts, renormalise their weights, and output $\sum_{i\in\text{top-}k} \tilde g_i\,\text{Expert}_i(x)$. This is sparse activation.

Worked: 8 experts, top-2 routing → active fraction 2/8 = 25% of expert parameters per token. If one expert has 134M parameters, the layer stores 1.07B but each token uses 268M. Total capacity is large; per-token compute is modest.

Everyday picture: a hospital with many specialists, where the front desk sends each patient to the two they need. Experts tend to specialise loosely (code tokens, punctuation, certain languages), learned automatically by the router.

sections.title: MoE memory and load balancing
sections.plain: All experts must sit in memory, and the router must be kept from overloading a few favourites.
sections.body:
Memory: MoE saves compute per token, not memory: all experts must be stored (and, in serving, loaded onto GPUs), even though few run. Communication between devices holding different experts adds overhead.

Load balancing: a router left alone tends to collapse onto a few experts, which get more training and become even more attractive while others stay unused. Systems add an auxiliary loss $E\sum_i f_i P_i$ (fraction of tokens routed to expert i × mean gate probability), which equals 1 when perfectly balanced and grows with skew; in ex2 a random router scores 1.165. Each expert also has a capacity (e.g. 1.25 × its fair share); tokens beyond it are dropped from that layer or rerouted.

So MoE trades simpler compute for engineering complexity: routing stability, balance, memory and communication must all be managed.

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• Attention variants (MQA/GQA) are also architecture changes, covered with the KV cache in M5.
  • Fine-grained and shared experts: some MoE designs use many small experts plus always-on shared experts.
  • Context extension with RoPE rescales the rotation frequencies so longer positions fall within the trained angle range.
  • QK-norm and other tweaks further stabilise very large training runs.

code.title: Normalisation, depth and RoPE
code.explain: Compares LayerNorm and RMSNorm on [2, −1, 3, 0], simulates 48 random layers to show how pre-norm and post-norm treat the residual stream, and implements RoPE to show that q·k is identical at positions (3, 1), (10, 8) and (105, 103) and that rotation preserves vector length.
mistakes: Rotating values as well as queries and keys.
Forgetting RMSNorm's learned gain in real models.
code.notes: Toy dimensions; real models use d = 4096 or more.
code.code:
"""LayerNorm vs RMSNorm, pre-norm vs post-norm depth behaviour, and RoPE's relative-position property."""
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

x = np.array([2.0, -1.0, 3.0, 0.0])
ln = (x - x.mean()) / np.sqrt(x.var() + 1e-6)
rms = x / np.sqrt((x ** 2).mean() + 1e-6)
print("x       ", x)
print("LayerNorm", ln, " (subtract mean 1.0, divide by std", round(float(x.std()), 3), ")")
print("RMSNorm  ", rms, " (divide by RMS", round(float(np.sqrt((x**2).mean())), 3), "; no mean subtraction)")

# Residual stream magnitude with many layers: post-norm normalises the stream, pre-norm only the branch input
d, L = 64, 48
def run(pre):
    h = rng.normal(size=d); norms = []
    for _ in range(L):
        W = rng.normal(size=(d, d)) / np.sqrt(d)
        nrm = lambda v: v / np.sqrt((v ** 2).mean())
        if pre: h = h + W @ np.tanh(nrm(h))          # x + F(Norm(x)): identity path untouched
        else:   h = nrm(h + W @ np.tanh(h))          # Norm(x + F(x))
        norms.append(np.sqrt((h ** 2).mean()))
    return norms
pre, post = run(True), run(False)
print(f"pre-norm residual RMS after 1, 12, 48 layers: {pre[0]:.2f}, {pre[11]:.2f}, {pre[47]:.2f} (clean identity path, gradients flow)")
print(f"post-norm residual RMS after 1, 12, 48 layers: {post[0]:.2f}, {post[11]:.2f}, {post[47]:.2f} (re-normalised every layer)")

# RoPE: rotate pairs of dimensions by angle m*theta_i
def rope(v, m, base=10000.0):
    d = len(v); out = v.copy()
    for i in range(d // 2):
        th = m * base ** (-2 * i / d); c, s = np.cos(th), np.sin(th)
        a, b = v[2 * i], v[2 * i + 1]
        out[2 * i], out[2 * i + 1] = a * c - b * s, a * s + b * c
    return out
q, k = rng.normal(size=8), rng.normal(size=8)
for (m, n) in [(3, 1), (10, 8), (105, 103), (5, 1)]:
    print(f"q at {m:3d}, k at {n:3d} (distance {m-n}): q·k = {rope(q, m) @ rope(k, n):+.4f}")
print("same distance -> same score, wherever the pair sits; norms unchanged:",
      round(float(np.linalg.norm(rope(q, 50))), 4), round(float(np.linalg.norm(q)), 4))

code.title: Activations, SwiGLU and Mixture of Experts
code.explain: Tabulates ReLU, GELU and SiLU, computes one plain-GELU and one SwiGLU feed-forward output and shows the 2/3-width parameter match (134.2M each at d = 4096), then routes 1,000 tokens through 8 experts with top-2 gating, reporting per-expert load and the balancing loss.
mistakes: Not renormalising the top-k gate weights.
Comparing SwiGLU and MLP at different parameter counts.
code.notes: Random weights; the point is the mechanics.
code.code:
"""GELU, GLU and SwiGLU; parameter-matched SwiGLU; Mixture-of-Experts top-2 routing and load balancing."""
import numpy as np
from math import erf, sqrt
rng = np.random.default_rng(1); np.set_printoptions(precision=3, suppress=True)

gelu = lambda z: 0.5 * z * (1 + erf(z / sqrt(2)))
silu = lambda z: z / (1 + np.exp(-z))
for z in (-2, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 2):
    print(f"z={z:+.1f}: ReLU {max(0, z):.3f}  GELU {gelu(z):+.3f}  SiLU/Swish {silu(z):+.3f}")

# One FFN position: plain GELU MLP vs SwiGLU (gate * up, then down)
d, h = 4, 8
x = rng.normal(size=d)
W1, W2 = rng.normal(size=(h, d)), rng.normal(size=(d, h))
Wg, Wu, Wd = rng.normal(size=(h, d)), rng.normal(size=(h, d)), rng.normal(size=(d, h))
plain = W2 @ np.array([gelu(v) for v in W1 @ x])
gate = silu(Wg @ x); up = Wu @ x
swiglu = Wd @ (gate * up)
print("gate values (how much of each hidden unit passes):", gate)
print("plain GELU FFN out:", plain, "| SwiGLU out:", swiglu)
dm = 4096
print(f"params: GELU FFN 2*d*4d = {2*dm*4*dm/1e6:.1f}M; SwiGLU 3*d*(8d/3) = {3*dm*int(8*dm/3)/1e6:.1f}M (hidden shrunk to 2/3 to match)")

# Mixture of Experts: 8 experts, top-2 routing
E, k, T = 8, 2, 1000
Wr = rng.normal(size=(E, d))
X = rng.normal(size=(T, d))
logits = X @ Wr.T
top = np.argsort(-logits, axis=1)[:, :k]
p = np.exp(logits - logits.max(1, keepdims=True)); p /= p.sum(1, keepdims=True)
print(f"active experts per token: {k}/{E} = {k/E:.0%}")
x0 = X[0]; t0 = top[0]; w = p[0, t0] / p[0, t0].sum()
print(f"token 0 -> experts {t0.tolist()} with weights {w.round(3).tolist()} (renormalised top-2 gate)")
load = np.bincount(top.ravel(), minlength=E) / (T * k)
print("share of routed slots per expert:", load.round(3), "(ideal 0.125 each)")
f, P = load, p.mean(0)
print(f"load-balancing loss  E * sum(f_i * P_i) = {E * (f * P).sum():.3f} (1.0 = perfectly balanced; higher = skewed)")
dense_ffn = 2 * 4096 * 16384
print(f"one expert FFN {dense_ffn/1e6:.0f}M params; 8 experts store {8*dense_ffn/1e6:.0f}M but each token uses {2*dense_ffn/1e6:.0f}M")
